items.title: L12: Urgent questions and statements to Parliament
items.source: Ministerial Code (announcing policy to Parliament first); House of Commons Procedure (urgent questions); Cabinet Office guidance on parliamentary business
items.body: The Ministerial Code says that when Parliament is in session, the most important announcements of government policy should be made in the first instance to Parliament. Ministers and officials therefore plan announcements so that Parliament hears first, not the press. The Speaker takes this seriously, and can criticise a minister who briefs the media in advance. An urgent question (UQ) is a request from an MP for a minister to come to the Commons and answer on a matter of urgent public importance. The Speaker decides whether to grant it, and the minister, or a junior minister, then attends, usually the same or the next day. Officials prepare quickly: a short opening statement if one is made, a Q&A brief covering likely questions, key facts and figures that have been checked, lines on anything sensitive, and a note of what the government has already said publicly. The brief should be accurate and should not mislead, since the minister answers to Parliament and any error must be corrected at the earliest opportunity. Statements made orally in the chamber are followed by questions from the opposition and backbenchers, and a copy of the text is often shared in advance with the opposition front bench, as a courtesy, shortly before delivery. Written ministerial statements are used for less urgent announcements and are published in Hansard. Officials should not give the media advance detail of a statement before the minister has delivered it, unless the minister has agreed in line with the rules.

questions.prompt: A department plans to announce a major policy change on Tuesday and Parliament is sitting. A journalist asks on Monday for the details. What should the press office do?

options.text: Hold the detail until the minister has told Parliament, in line with the Code
Give an off-the-record briefing, because the story is likely to come out anyway
Release the embargoed text to trusted outlets so that the coverage is accurate
Confirm the main points but not the figures, which are the sensitive part

questions.hint: Important announcements go to Parliament first when it is sitting.

questions.prompt: The Speaker grants an urgent question on a topic your team covers, for the following morning. What should the team do first?

options.text: Ask the Speaker's office to defer it until a full policy paper is ready
Draft a detailed options paper so that the minister can decide the answer
Gather checked facts and prepare a short Q&A brief at speed
Pass the request to the press office to answer by media statement

questions.hint: A UQ needs accurate, checked briefing delivered quickly.

questions.prompt: While preparing for an urgent question an official finds that a figure in an earlier public statement was wrong. What is the best course?

options.text: Avoid using the figure and say nothing about the earlier error
Tell the private office at once so the record can be corrected
Use the right figure in the brief but leave the earlier statement alone
Wait to see whether the minister is challenged on the figure

questions.hint: Errors must be corrected at the earliest opportunity, which starts with telling the minister.

questions.prompt: How does an oral ministerial statement differ from a written ministerial statement?

options.text: Oral statements are reserved for the Prime Minister; written ones are for other ministers
Written statements go privately to MPs, while oral statements are published in Hansard
Oral statements cover domestic policy, while written statements cover foreign affairs
Oral statements are made in the chamber with questions; written ones publish less urgent announcements

questions.hint: The choice depends on how significant and urgent the announcement is.

questions.prompt: An MP applies for an urgent question on Monday morning. What decides whether a minister must come to the House to answer it?

options.text: The Speaker decides whether it is granted
The minister chooses whether to attend, since ministers set their own diaries
The Leader of the House allocates time to each question on the day
The Chief Whip agrees which questions the government will answer

questions.hint: The Speaker decides whether an urgent question is granted.

questions.prompt: A minister plans to give a newspaper an exclusive the night before announcing a policy to the House. What is the problem?

options.text: There is no problem, because ministers may brief any outlet while a decision is still confidential
Ministers may brief the press early only on matters that involve no spending decision
It is a matter for the party's press team and falls outside the Ministerial Code
It risks breaching the expectation that Parliament is told first, and the Speaker may criticise it

questions.hint: The Code expects significant announcements to reach Parliament first.

questions.prompt: An official drafts the minister's opening statement for an urgent question. Which feature matters most?

options.text: It is persuasive enough to win over the opposition benches in the debate
It is accurate, checked and consistent with earlier statements
It is long enough to use the time and so reduce supplementary questions
It avoids numbers, which the minister could be challenged on afterwards

questions.hint: Accuracy and consistency matter most because the minister answers to Parliament.

questions.prompt: Why might the text of a statement be shared with the opposition front bench shortly before it is delivered?

options.text: Because the opposition front bench must approve the text before delivery
Because the Speaker requires the opposition to certify the figures
As a courtesy, so that opposition spokespeople can prepare to respond
Because a statement of this kind is a joint statement of both front benches

questions.hint: Sharing the text shortly before delivery is a courtesy practice.

items.title: L12: How a Bill becomes law and what officials do
items.source: UK Parliament, How a Bill becomes law; Cabinet Office, Guide to Making Legislation
items.body: Most primary legislation starts as a Bill. A Bill introduced in either House normally goes through the same stages. First reading is a formality. At second reading the House debates the main principles. In committee stage the detail is examined line by line, often by a public bill committee in the Commons, and amendments are considered. At report stage the whole House can consider further amendments, and third reading is a final debate. The Bill then passes to the other House, where it goes through similar stages. If the two Houses disagree on amendments, the Bill can pass between them, sometimes called ping-pong, until they agree. When both Houses have agreed the same text, the Bill receives Royal Assent and becomes an Act of Parliament. Behind this process is a department's Bill team, made up of policy officials, lawyers, a Bill manager, and Parliamentary Counsel, who are specialist lawyers who draft legislation based on instructions from the department. Officials produce explanatory notes, support ministers in the chamber, prepare briefing for each stage, and track amendments. Government Bills are cleared through the Cabinet's legislative programme before introduction, and the policy must have collective agreement. Officials also consider whether the Bill touches devolved matters, requiring the consent of devolved legislatures under the Sewel convention, and consider the Bill's human rights and equality implications. After Royal Assent, further work is needed for commencement, the date on which provisions take effect, and for any secondary legislation the Act enables.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly orders the main Bill stages in the first House?

options.text: Committee stage, second reading, report stage, third reading
Second reading, report stage, committee stage, third reading
Third reading, committee stage, second reading, report stage
Second reading, committee stage, report stage, third reading

questions.hint: Principles are debated first, then detail, then the final reading.

questions.prompt: The Lords amend a Commons Bill and the Commons disagrees with the amendment. What typically happens next?

options.text: The Lords' amendments take effect unless the Commons rejects them within a week
The Bill passes between the Houses until both agree the same text
The Bill lapses and must be introduced again as a new Bill
The Speaker chooses which House's wording becomes the law

questions.hint: Both Houses must agree the same text before Royal Assent.

questions.prompt: What do Parliamentary Counsel do in a department's Bill team?

options.text: Decide the government's policy that the Bill is to carry out
Represent the department if the resulting Act is challenged in court
Draft the Bill from instructions given by the policy officials
Advise the Speaker on how the Bill should be handled in the chamber

questions.hint: Parliamentary Counsel are specialist drafters who work from policy instructions.

questions.prompt: What does Royal Assent do?

options.text: It turns a Bill that both Houses have agreed into an Act of Parliament
It allows the Bill to be introduced in the second House after the Commons passes it
It confirms that the Bill has public support following consultation
It brings every provision of the Act into force on the same day

questions.hint: Royal Assent completes the passage of the Bill, though commencement may come later.

questions.prompt: An Act received Royal Assent in March, but a department says one section 'is not yet in force'. What explains this?

options.text: A devolved legislature vetoed the section under the Sewel convention
The section must first be approved by the Public Accounts Committee
Commencement: provisions take effect when brought into force, which may be later
The Speaker has ordered a delay for the section pending a review

questions.hint: Provisions may be brought into force by commencement later.

questions.prompt: Why do officials prepare explanatory notes for a Bill?

options.text: To explain what the Bill's provisions mean and are intended to do, for readers
To replace the Bill's wording where amendments are made at committee stage or report stage
To set out the political case that the minister wants made for the Bill
To list the amendments that were rejected at each stage

questions.hint: Explanatory notes explain the Bill, though they are not part of it.

questions.prompt: A Bill covers a topic that is partly devolved. What should officials do?

options.text: Proceed as normal, since Parliament can legislate for any matter
Wait until Royal Assent and then ask devolved ministers to approve the Act
Ask the Speaker to certify whether the Bill touches devolved matters
Engage early with the devolved governments so that legislative consent can be sought where needed

questions.hint: Under Sewel, consent is normally sought for legislation on devolved matters.

questions.prompt: What do ministers normally need before a government Bill is introduced?

options.text: A vote of approval from the opposition front bench on the principle
Collective clearance of the policy and a place in the legislative programme
A report from the National Audit Office on the Bill's costs
Clearance from the Civil Service Commission that the policy is politically impartial

questions.hint: Bills are cleared collectively before they are introduced.

items.title: L12: Secondary legislation and statutory instruments
items.source: UK Parliament, Statutory Instruments; Cabinet Office, Guide to Making Legislation; Statutory Instruments Act 1946
items.body: Secondary legislation, also called delegated legislation, is law made by ministers or other bodies using powers given by an Act of Parliament, called the parent or enabling Act. Most of it takes the form of statutory instruments (SIs). It is used for detail and for matters that need to change often, such as rates, forms or technical rules, so that Parliament does not have to pass a new Act each time. The parent Act says what procedure applies. Under the negative procedure, an SI becomes law unless either House passes a motion to annul it within a set period, usually forty days. Under the affirmative procedure, it must be approved by a vote in Parliament, often in both Houses, before it takes effect or continues. Some SIs have no procedure beyond being laid, and some are made urgently and then approved afterwards. Parliament's committees examine SIs: the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments checks technical points, such as whether the instrument is within the powers given, while the Lords Secondary Legislation Scrutiny Committee considers policy implications. Officials prepare the SI itself, an explanatory memorandum setting out the purpose, impact and consultation, and often an impact assessment. They must check that the instrument is within the powers of the parent Act, because an instrument that goes beyond them is vulnerable to challenge in the courts. Wide powers allowing ministers to amend primary legislation, often called Henry VIII powers, attract particular scrutiny.

questions.prompt: Under the negative procedure, what happens to a statutory instrument if nobody objects within the period?

options.text: It lapses unless both Houses approve it within the period
It goes to the Speaker, who decides whether it should continue
It becomes or remains law without a vote
It must be laid again in the next session before it has effect

questions.hint: Under the negative procedure an SI stands unless it is annulled.

questions.prompt: A department's new SI is subject to the affirmative procedure. What must happen before it can take effect or continue?

options.text: It must lie before Parliament for forty days with no motion against it
The Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments must certify its policy
The Speaker must confirm it is within the minister's powers
Parliament must approve it, usually by a vote

questions.hint: Affirmative means positive approval is required.

questions.prompt: What determines which parliamentary procedure applies to an SI?

options.text: The minister's choice, depending on how contentious the instrument is
The enabling Act, which says what procedure applies to instruments made under it
The Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments, after it has examined the draft and reported
The Treasury, according to the spending the instrument involves

questions.hint: The parent Act sets the procedure.

questions.prompt: A draft SI would require something that the enabling Act does not clearly allow. What is the main risk if it is made anyway?

options.text: It could be challenged in court as going beyond the powers the Act gives
It would be treated as primary legislation once it is approved
Only the explanatory memorandum would need correcting before it is laid
It would be approved automatically by the Joint Committee on the minister's authority

questions.hint: An SI must stay within the powers in the parent Act.

questions.prompt: What does the Joint Committee on Statutory Instruments mainly check?

options.text: Whether the policy behind the instrument is wise, fair and has public support
Whether the department has the funding needed to implement it
Technical points, including whether the instrument is within the powers given
Whether the minister consulted widely before making it

questions.hint: It scrutinises technical matters rather than policy merits.

questions.prompt: An Act lets a minister change a fee each year by SI, not by a new Act. What is the main reason for this?

options.text: Parliament has no power to legislate about fees
Primary legislation is not allowed to contain figures or rates
It avoids any parliamentary scrutiny of the change
Details that change often are better handled without a new Act each time

questions.hint: Delegated powers allow detail to be updated without new Acts.

questions.prompt: What should an explanatory memorandum to an SI do?

options.text: Argue the minister's party case for the instrument in plain language
Explain the instrument's purpose, effects and consultation for Parliament and the public
List every amendment Parliament has proposed to the instrument
Replace the legal text with a plain English summary

questions.hint: The memorandum explains the instrument to Parliament and the public.

questions.prompt: Why are Henry VIII powers controversial?

options.text: They allow ministers to amend or repeal primary legislation by secondary legislation
They let ministers dismiss civil servants without following the normal disciplinary process
They allow the Crown to withhold Royal Assent from an Act
They stop the courts from reviewing the lawfulness of an instrument

questions.hint: They give ministers wide power over Acts, so they attract close scrutiny.

items.title: L12: The Public Sector Equality Duty in decisions
items.source: Equality Act 2010, section 149; Equality and Human Rights Commission guidance on the Public Sector Equality Duty
items.body: Section 149 of the Equality Act 2010 places a duty on public authorities, including government departments, to have due regard to three aims when carrying out their functions. They are eliminating unlawful discrimination, harassment and victimisation, advancing equality of opportunity between people who share a protected characteristic and those who do not, and fostering good relations between them. The nine protected characteristics are age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation, though the duty to have due regard to marriage and civil partnership applies only to the first aim. The duty is not a duty to achieve a particular result; it is a duty to think about the issues properly and to weigh them in decision-making. Courts have said that due regard must be exercised in substance, with rigour and with an open mind, before and at the time a decision is taken, not as a justification after the event. It cannot be delegated to someone else, so the decision-maker must be properly informed. Equality impact assessments are the usual way to record the analysis, though the law does not demand a particular format. Officials should consider evidence, consult those affected where appropriate, identify possible effects on different groups, consider mitigation, and keep a record. A failure to comply can lead to a challenge by judicial review, and decisions may be quashed. Officials should raise the duty early, since leaving it until late in a process makes it harder to change course.

questions.prompt: A policy decision has been made, and an official then writes an equality assessment to support it. What is the problem?

options.text: Nothing, because any equality assessment on file meets the duty whenever it is written
Due regard must be paid before and at the time of the decision, not afterwards
The assessment should have been signed off by the Treasury before it was used
The duty applies only to recruitment, so a policy decision falls outside it

questions.hint: The duty requires real consideration at the time of the decision.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the three aims in section 149 of the Equality Act?

options.text: Guaranteeing equal outcomes for every group in each policy area
Reducing public spending on services used by protected groups
Ensuring that every public body employs equal numbers from each group
Advancing equality of opportunity between people who do and do not share a protected characteristic

questions.hint: The aims concern discrimination, equality of opportunity and good relations.

questions.prompt: A department weighs the effects of a policy on disabled people, records its analysis and goes ahead, although some will be worse off. What is the position on the duty?

options.text: It is breached, because the duty prohibits any policy that disadvantages a protected group
It is met only if the Equality and Human Rights Commission approves the decision
The duty is about due regard, not guaranteed results, so it may have been met
It is met only if a majority of those affected support the policy

questions.hint: The duty requires proper consideration, not a particular result.

questions.prompt: How have the courts described the right way to approach due regard?

options.text: Genuine consideration of the equality effects, with rigour and an open mind
Quoting section 149 in the decision paper to show the duty was known
Asking an outside adviser to carry out the duty in place of the decision-maker
Considering equality once at the start of a project and not revisiting it

questions.hint: Courts look at whether the duty was exercised in substance.

questions.prompt: An official proposes leaving the equality analysis until the end of a long policy process. What is the main risk?

options.text: The analysis will be too long for the minister to read
The Equality and Human Rights Commission can fine the department automatically
It will be hard to change course, and the decision may be open to challenge
The minister will not be able to rely on any analysis that arrives late

questions.hint: Early consideration makes the duty meaningful and the policy better.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely consequence of a decision that did not comply with the duty?

options.text: It is void automatically, without the need for any court order
The Equality and Human Rights Commission takes over the decision
The minister must resign under the Ministerial Code
It may be challenged by judicial review and the decision quashed

questions.hint: Non-compliance can lead to a successful judicial review.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a protected characteristic under the Equality Act 2010?

options.text: Gender reassignment
Political opinion
Income level
Place of residence

questions.hint: Nine characteristics are protected under the Act.

questions.prompt: Why is an equality impact assessment useful to a decision-maker?

options.text: It guarantees the decision cannot later be challenged by judicial review or the courts
It records the evidence considered, the likely effects and any mitigation
It is required by the Act in a prescribed form that must be used
It replaces the need to consult the people who are affected

questions.hint: It records due regard, though the law prescribes no format.

items.title: L12: Judicial review and the duty of candour
items.source: Civil Procedure Rules, Pre-Action Protocol for Judicial Review; Government Legal Department guidance; Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985]
items.body: Judicial review is the process by which a court examines whether a public body has acted lawfully in making a decision. It does not decide whether the decision was right on the merits; it asks whether the decision-maker had the power, followed a fair procedure and acted rationally. Three traditional grounds are illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety, which include acting beyond the law's powers, reaching a decision no reasonable authority could reach, and failing to give a fair hearing or follow required steps. Other grounds include breach of a legitimate expectation and failure to consider relevant matters. A claimant normally has to act promptly and in any event within three months of the decision. Before starting a claim, a claimant usually sends a pre-action letter setting out the complaint, and the department must reply within a short period, with its position and the documents it relies on. If the court quashes a decision, the decision-maker may have to retake it lawfully, and the same outcome may be reached again by a proper process. The government and public bodies owe a duty of candour in judicial review: they must disclose material that is relevant to the issues, including documents that are unhelpful to their case, and give a full and fair account of how the decision was taken. Officials should keep records, and when a claim is expected, must preserve relevant documents and avoid deleting emails or notes. Legal advisers will usually run the case, but officials must provide accurate evidence and take part in drafting witness statements.

questions.prompt: A department is told that a claim for judicial review is expected over a recent decision. What should officials do about their emails and notes?

options.text: Tidy the files so that only the formal record and the final signed papers remain
Delete personal notes so the formal record is the single source
Preserve relevant documents and avoid deleting anything about the decision
Wait for the court to order disclosure before taking any steps

questions.hint: Preservation of records is part of acting candidly in litigation.

questions.prompt: What question does a court ask in a judicial review?

options.text: Whether the court would have reached the same decision on the evidence
Whether the decision-maker acted lawfully, fairly and rationally, not whether it was best
Whether the policy behind the decision commands public support
Whether the minister acted in the interests of the governing party

questions.hint: Judicial review looks at lawfulness, not the merits.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a traditional ground of judicial review?

options.text: Unpopularity, because the decision was widely disliked by those it affects
Cost overrun, because the decision cost far more than was budgeted
Delegation, because a minister's decision was taken by an official
Procedural impropriety, such as failing to follow a fair process

questions.hint: Illegality, irrationality and procedural impropriety are the traditional grounds.

questions.prompt: What does the duty of candour require of a public body defending a judicial review?

options.text: Disclose relevant material, including documents that do not help its own case
Disclose only the documents that support the decision that was taken and the reasons given
Stay silent on anything the claimant has not specifically asked for
Publish its legal advice so the public can see why it acted

questions.hint: A public body must give a full and fair account of how it decided.

questions.prompt: How quickly must a claim for judicial review normally be brought?

options.text: Promptly, and in any event within three months of the decision
Within six years of the decision, as with most civil claims
Within one year of the decision, in line with human rights claims
At any time, provided internal appeals have been exhausted

questions.hint: Judicial review has a short time limit.

questions.prompt: A court quashes a decision because the procedure was unfair. What may the decision-maker do next?

options.text: Treat the ruling as advisory and rely on the original decision
Ask the court to choose the outcome that should now be adopted
Have the minister overrule the court's order by a new direction
Retake the decision through a lawful process, which may reach the same outcome

questions.hint: A quashing order usually means the decision must be retaken lawfully.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the pre-action protocol for judicial review?

options.text: To allow the court to decide the case on the papers without a hearing
To give the claimant extra time beyond the three-month limit
To encourage an exchange of positions and possible settlement before a claim is filed
To send the dispute to the Ombudsman before the court can hear it

questions.hint: It encourages early exchange of positions and possible settlement.

questions.prompt: An official is asked for a witness statement in a claim. What should it contain?

options.text: A defence of the minister's policy, written to persuade the court
An accurate account of how the decision was reached, drawn from the records
The official's personal view on the merits of the claimant's case
Only the facts that support the department's position in the claim, to protect it

questions.hint: Evidence must be truthful and complete, consistent with candour.

items.title: L12: Public appointments and the Governance Code
items.source: Cabinet Office, Governance Code for Public Appointments; Office of the Commissioner for Public Appointments
items.body: Ministers appoint the chairs and members of many public bodies, such as regulators, advisory committees and boards of arm's length bodies. To ensure public confidence, these appointments follow the Governance Code for Public Appointments. The Code is built on the principle that appointments should be made on merit, after a fair and open competition, and that the process should be proportionate to the importance of the role. The Commissioner for Public Appointments is independent of government and is responsible for regulating and monitoring the process, publishing an annual report, and investigating complaints. For significant appointments, an advisory assessment panel is formed, with a panel chair who is usually an independent member, and panel members who include departmental officials and sometimes experts. The panel assesses applications against criteria, interviews candidates, and reports to the minister on who is appointable, often with a ranked or unranked list. The minister then chooses from appointable candidates; they may meet candidates before deciding, but they cannot select someone who the panel has not found appointable without following the rules. Ministers must also consider diversity and the conflicts of interest of candidates, and, for certain roles, a pre-appointment hearing may be held by a select committee. Political activity of candidates is declared but is not a bar to appointment, though the appointment must still be based on merit. Departments publish roles on the Public Appointments website, and keep records so that decisions can be justified. Officials who support the process should be careful to keep it impartial, and report any approach by a minister or special adviser that bypasses the rules.

questions.prompt: A minister wants to appoint a friend as chair of a body and asks officials to skip the competition. What should the official do?

options.text: Skip the competition if the minister gives the instruction in writing
Explain that the Code requires a fair and open competition on merit, and escalate
Run a competition for show, with the friend named in advance as the intended winner
Add the friend to the shortlist without assessing them against the criteria

questions.hint: The Code requires merit-based appointment through a fair and open process.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the Commissioner for Public Appointments?

options.text: To choose the chair of each public body after the panel has interviewed all the candidates
To advise ministers on which candidate to prefer in each competition
To represent departments when appointments are challenged in court
To regulate and monitor the appointments process and investigate complaints

questions.hint: The Commissioner is independent and regulates the process.

questions.prompt: After an advisory assessment panel has met, what does it normally give the minister?

options.text: A report on which candidates are appointable, from which the minister chooses
A single name, which the minister is required to appoint
A list of candidates whom the minister must reject on merit grounds
A scored league table that the minister must follow in strict order

questions.hint: The minister chooses from candidates found appointable.

questions.prompt: How is a candidate's political activity treated in a public appointment?

options.text: It automatically disqualifies the candidate from any public appointment
It is kept from the panel so as not to influence them
It is declared and made public, but is not a bar to appointment
It is irrelevant and must never be recorded

questions.hint: Political activity is declared, but merit is the test.

questions.prompt: What does appointment 'on merit' mean?

options.text: Choosing the candidate best able to meet the role's criteria in a fair competition
Choosing the candidate with the strongest record of loyalty to the government of the day
Choosing the candidate recommended by the outgoing chair of the body
Choosing the candidate with the longest service on public bodies

questions.hint: Merit means judged against criteria in a fair process.

questions.prompt: Why does an advisory panel for a significant role often include an independent member?

options.text: To speed up the process by removing the need for a minister's decision
To represent the main political parties during the interviews
To give confidence that the process is fair and not controlled by the department or minister
To approve the minister's chosen candidate before the offer is made

questions.hint: Independence increases trust in the process.

questions.prompt: What is a pre-appointment hearing for some senior public roles?

options.text: A hearing held by the Civil Service Commission for unsuccessful candidates
A select committee hearing with the minister's preferred candidate before appointment
A meeting at the Cabinet Office to agree the pay of the chosen candidate
A review by the panel chair of the minister's reasons for rejecting any of the candidates

questions.hint: Select committees may hold hearings with preferred candidates for some roles.

questions.prompt: A candidate has an undeclared business link with a supplier to the body. What should the process do?

options.text: Treat it as private, because a candidate's business interests are not a matter for the panel
Remove the candidate silently and without giving a reason
Confirm the appointment first and ask about interests once the chair has started
Identify and manage the conflict before any appointment is confirmed

questions.hint: Conflicts of interest need to be declared and managed.

items.title: L12: Regulators and independence from ministers
items.source: Cabinet Office, Public Bodies guidance; Regulators' Code; Legislative and Regulatory Reform Act 2006
items.body: Many regulators, such as those covering energy, finance, communications and health, are established by Act of Parliament and given powers by law. They are accountable to Parliament, and usually sponsored by a government department, but their statutory duties mean that ministers cannot direct their decisions in individual cases. The usual pattern is that ministers and Parliament decide the framework: they set the law, the regulator's objectives and duties, its budget and sometimes issue a statement of strategic priorities which the regulator must have regard to. The regulator decides how to carry out its functions, including licensing, enforcement and price setting, within that framework. Independence helps maintain trust, since decisions on enforcement or on prices should not appear to be politically influenced. A minister who sees a problem may ask the regulator for information, discuss policy, change the law or appoint new board members when terms end, but should not ask it to reach a particular result in a case. Regulators remain accountable: their decisions can be appealed, subject to judicial review, scrutinised by select committees and audited by the NAO, and they report annually. The Regulators' Code, which statutory regulators must have regard to, says that they should support compliant growth, base their approach on risk and be open about their activities. The sponsor department has a role to monitor performance, advise on appointments and funding, and review whether the framework is working. Officials should avoid any contact which could look like interference in a live case, and keep a record of contacts with regulators.

questions.prompt: A minister is unhappy with an enforcement decision a regulator has made against a company. What is the proper route?

options.text: Discuss policy or consider changing the framework, but not direct the case
Instruct the regulator to reverse the decision using the sponsoring department's authority
Ask officials to raise concerns informally with the regulator's staff until it relents
Publish a statement saying the decision should be set aside

questions.hint: Ministers can change the law but cannot direct individual decisions.

questions.prompt: What might a statement of strategic priorities do for a regulator?

options.text: Order the regulator to reach set outcomes in each case it considers
Set out government priorities the regulator must have regard to, without directing cases
Replace the regulator's statutory duties with the minister's own
Give the minister power to overrule the regulator's board decisions

questions.hint: Strategic statements shape direction but do not determine cases.

questions.prompt: How can a regulator's decision be challenged?

options.text: Only by a vote of Parliament to annul the decision
By the minister amending the decision using the sponsor department's powers
By a direction from the Cabinet Office, which can quash decisions
By appeal where the law provides one, or by judicial review

questions.hint: Regulators remain subject to the law and the courts.

questions.prompt: Which of these does a sponsor department typically do for a regulator?

options.text: Approve each enforcement decision before the regulator announces it
Chair the regulator's board meetings to represent the minister
Monitor performance, advise on appointments and funding, and review the framework
Set penalties in individual cases where the regulator is unsure

questions.hint: The sponsor oversees the framework, not individual decisions.

questions.prompt: An official sponsoring a regulator receives a call from a company under investigation. What should the official do?

options.text: Offer to raise the company's concerns informally with the regulator
Tell the company what the regulator has said to the department about the case
Assure the company that the department will not back enforcement
Explain that the matter is for the regulator and keep a note of the contact

questions.hint: Officials must avoid anything that looks like interference in a live case.

questions.prompt: What does the Regulators' Code ask regulators to do?

options.text: Set penalties at the highest level to deter misconduct
Support compliant growth, take a risk-based approach and be open about their activities
Follow ministers' preferences when deciding individual cases
Keep enforcement activity confidential to protect businesses

questions.hint: The Code promotes proportionate, risk-based, transparent regulation.

questions.prompt: Why does regulatory independence matter?

options.text: It prevents Parliament from changing the regulator's powers
It exempts the regulator from audit and parliamentary scrutiny
It maintains trust that decisions rest on evidence and law, not political pressure
It lets the regulator set its own budget without Treasury involvement

questions.hint: Independence supports confidence in impartial decisions.

questions.prompt: Which of these may a minister legitimately do in relation to a regulator?

options.text: Appoint board members when terms end, following public appointments rules
Order a fine in a particular case where the minister thinks one is deserved
Veto an enforcement decision by private letter to the chair
Instruct the regulator to pause an investigation while the minister considers policy

questions.hint: Appointments are one of the levers ministers have, within the rules.

items.title: L12: Security classifications and need to know
items.source: Cabinet Office, Government Security Classifications Policy; Government Functional Standard GovS 007: Security; HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard
items.body: Government information is classified into three levels: OFFICIAL, SECRET and TOP SECRET. Most government work is OFFICIAL, which covers routine business and operations. Some OFFICIAL information is particularly sensitive, for example personal data, commercially sensitive material or sensitive policy, and can be marked with the handling caveat OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, which signals that extra care is needed, though it is not a separate classification. SECRET covers information that could seriously harm national security, military capabilities or international relations if compromised, and TOP SECRET covers the most sensitive information, where compromise could cause exceptionally grave damage. The classification determines how information must be stored, shared and disposed of. A key principle is need to know: access should depend on a person's role, not only on their security clearance or seniority. Having a clearance does not mean you may see everything at that level. Another is that aggregation of lots of OFFICIAL information can raise its sensitivity, and so a combined dataset may need more protection than each part. Personnel security checks match the sensitivity of work: the Baseline Personnel Security Standard is a minimum set of checks for all staff, while Counter-Terrorist Check, Security Check and Developed Vetting are the clearance levels for more sensitive roles. Officials should classify what they create thoughtfully, not over-classifying or under-classifying, and mark it so others know how to handle it. If information is lost or sent to the wrong person, it should be reported promptly through the department's security incident process, because early reporting limits the harm.

questions.prompt: An official with Security Check clearance asks to see a SECRET document that has nothing to do with their work. What is the right response?

options.text: Allow it, since their clearance level covers SECRET material and they are trusted
Allow it if they promise not to share the contents
Refuse, because access depends on need to know as well as clearance
Allow it if their line manager is at a more senior grade

questions.hint: Clearance alone does not give a right of access.

questions.prompt: What is OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE?

options.text: A handling caveat for OFFICIAL information needing extra care, not a separate level
A fourth classification sitting between OFFICIAL and SECRET
A marking showing that the information may be released under FOI
A marking that restricts the information to ministers and special advisers

questions.hint: OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE is a caveat, not a fourth level.

questions.prompt: A team combines many individual OFFICIAL records about named people into one spreadsheet. What should they consider?

options.text: There is no extra risk, since each record is OFFICIAL and a total cannot be higher
The combined dataset may be more sensitive than each part and need extra protection
The spreadsheet automatically becomes TOP SECRET once it passes a size limit
It stops being government information once personal details are combined

questions.hint: Aggregation can raise sensitivity.

questions.prompt: An official sends a document with personal data to the wrong recipient by mistake. What should they do?

options.text: Ask the recipient to delete it and keep the matter between the two of them for now
Wait to see whether the recipient replies before telling anyone
Resend the correct version and say nothing about the first message
Report it promptly through the security incident process and try to recall it

questions.hint: Early reporting limits the harm.

questions.prompt: What is the Baseline Personnel Security Standard?

options.text: The highest level of vetting, used for the most sensitive posts
The minimum set of pre-employment checks for those with access to government assets
A check that applies only to ministers and special advisers
A check that applies only to staff working overseas

questions.hint: BPSS is the baseline set of checks.

questions.prompt: How should an official decide the classification of a document they create?

options.text: Choose the highest level available, to be safe
Leave it unmarked and let the recipient decide how it should be treated later
Consider the impact if it were compromised and apply the matching level
Choose the level that matches the author's own grade

questions.hint: Over-classifying and under-classifying are both problems.

questions.prompt: Which marking applies to information whose compromise could cause exceptionally grave damage?

options.text: TOP SECRET
SECRET
OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE
CONFIDENTIAL

questions.hint: TOP SECRET is the highest classification.

questions.prompt: Why does need to know matter even among colleagues who are cleared?

options.text: It ensures managers can see everything that their teams see
It makes information available to anyone with the right clearance
It applies only when information is shared outside government
It limits the risk of disclosure by keeping access to people who need the information

questions.hint: Limiting access reduces risk.

items.title: L12: Supply, Estimates and budget controls: DEL and AME
items.source: HM Treasury, Managing Public Money, Supply Estimates guidance; HM Treasury, Consolidated Budgeting Guidance
items.body: Parliament controls the money the government may spend. Each year departments publish Main Estimates, which set out the resources and cash they ask Parliament to authorise. The House of Commons approves them through the Supply procedure, and legislation, known as the Supply and Appropriation Act, gives them legal effect. Supplementary Estimates, usually in the winter and spring, allow departments to ask for changes to what was agreed. A department cannot lawfully spend beyond the limits authorised by Parliament, and spending without authority is irregular. Within government, spending is controlled in two categories. Departmental Expenditure Limits (DEL) cover planned spending that the department can control, such as running costs and programmes, and are set for several years at a Spending Review. Annually Managed Expenditure (AME) covers spending that is demand-led or hard to control in the short term, such as benefits, debt interest and some pension costs, and is forecast and monitored rather than capped in the same way. Spending is also divided into resource, which covers day-to-day running costs such as pay, and capital, which covers investment in assets such as buildings and equipment. Moving money between those categories needs Treasury agreement, because the rules protect capital investment from being used to pay for day-to-day costs. Departments cannot normally carry over unspent budget without Treasury agreement. Officials working on budgets should keep within control totals, identify pressures early, and explain forecasts honestly. An overspend against a Parliamentary limit is a serious matter for the accounting officer, who may be called to explain it to the Public Accounts Committee.

questions.prompt: A team realises it will overspend its resource budget this year. What should it do?

options.text: Wait until year end in case underspends elsewhere cover it
Move money from the capital budget, since it is the same department
Defer the invoices to next year so the figures look balanced
Raise it early with the finance director so options can be agreed, with the Treasury if needed

questions.hint: Early escalation allows proper options to be found.

questions.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be classed as AME rather than DEL?

options.text: Staff salaries in the department
A planned new IT system
Demand-led spending such as certain benefits
Office accommodation costs

questions.hint: AME covers demand-led spending that is hard to control.

questions.prompt: Which spending would normally count as capital rather than resource?

options.text: Buying equipment or buildings that last several years
Paying staff salaries
Paying monthly utility bills
Paying for stationery and postage

questions.hint: Capital means investment in assets.

questions.prompt: What do Main Estimates do?

options.text: Report the department's performance against its published targets for the financial year
Ask Parliament to authorise the resources and cash needed for the year
Publish the NAO's opinion on the previous year's accounts
Record the spending actually incurred in the previous year

questions.hint: Estimates ask Parliament to authorise spending.

questions.prompt: Why does the Treasury control moves between capital and resource budgets?

options.text: To stop investment budgets being used for day-to-day costs without agreement
To make the accounts simpler for the National Audit Office to audit and report on
To prevent departments from buying buildings or equipment
To keep all spending on pay within the Cabinet Office's limit

questions.hint: The rules protect capital investment.

questions.prompt: What is the status of spending that goes beyond a limit set by Parliament?

options.text: It is acceptable if the purpose was good and the outcomes were achieved
It is approved automatically after the end of the year
It is treated as a minor matter if it is under one per cent of budget
It is irregular, and the accounting officer may have to explain it

questions.hint: Parliament's limits are legal controls on spending.

questions.prompt: What does a Spending Review do?

options.text: Sets the annual rates of benefit payments for the coming year
Sets multi-year departmental budgets, including DEL, for the government
Audits departments' accounts and reports on regularity
Decides the funding for the devolved governments alone

questions.hint: Spending Reviews set DEL across several years.

questions.prompt: A department has an underspend at year end. What is the usual position on carrying it forward?

options.text: It is carried over in full, as the budget belongs to the department
It must be returned to the Cabinet Office, which reallocates it
It cannot normally be carried over without Treasury agreement
It is held by the NAO until the accounts have been audited

questions.hint: Unspent budget is not generally carried over without agreement.

items.title: L12: Unauthorised disclosure and leaks
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; National Security Act 2023; Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body: Civil servants have a duty of confidentiality about the information they handle in their work. The Civil Service Code requires them to keep information secure and not to disclose official information without authority, and the Official Secrets Act 1989 makes it a criminal offence to disclose certain categories of information without lawful authority, including security and intelligence, defence, international relations and crime. The National Security Act 2023 replaced the older Official Secrets Acts of 1911, 1920 and 1939 and created offences relating to espionage and foreign interference, though the 1989 Act remains in force. A leak is the unauthorised disclosure of information to the media or others. Leaks can damage trust between ministers and officials, harm negotiations, endanger individuals, and breach the law. Departments investigate serious leaks, which may include checking who had access to the information. Staff should cooperate with a proper investigation, and may be disciplined or dismissed for a breach. Civil servants who have concerns about something they see have lawful routes to raise them. The Civil Service Code allows them to report matters to their line manager, a senior manager or a nominated officer, and then to the Civil Service Commission, and the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 protects workers who make qualifying disclosures in the proper way. Telling the press first is not normally a protected route, and may result in sanctions. Officials should also be careful about speaking about their work in public, including on social media, and should check any planned publication or speaking engagement about their work with their line management.

questions.prompt: An official sees a draft policy on a colleague's desk and is tempted to tell a journalist friend. Why should they not?

options.text: Journalists are not allowed to receive information from civil servants working in government departments
Draft policies are never classified, so any draft can be shared
It is allowed if the friend promises not to publish the details
It would be an unauthorised disclosure, breaching the Code and possibly the law

questions.hint: Unauthorised disclosure breaches the duty of confidentiality.

questions.prompt: Which Act makes some unauthorised disclosures by civil servants a criminal offence?

options.text: The Freedom of Information Act 2000
The Official Secrets Act 1989
The Public Records Act 1958
The Equality Act 2010

questions.hint: The 1989 Act criminalises certain unauthorised disclosures.

questions.prompt: A civil servant has serious concerns that a department is acting unlawfully. What is the proper first route?

options.text: Raise it with their line manager, a senior manager or a nominated officer
Contact a journalist, since the press can act more quickly
Post about it on social media so the public can judge
Wait until they have left the department and then speak out

questions.hint: The Code sets out internal routes first.

questions.prompt: Which Act replaced the Official Secrets Acts of 1911, 1920 and 1939?

options.text: The Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
The Data Protection Act 2018
The National Security Act 2023
The Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010

questions.hint: The 2023 Act replaced them but not the 1989 Act.

questions.prompt: What may happen when a department investigates a leak?

options.text: The inquiry must stop if the source is not identified within a few weeks
The inquiry must publish the names of everyone who had access
The inquiry cannot ask staff any questions without a court order
It may check who had access to the information, and staff are expected to cooperate

questions.hint: Investigations can examine access and expect cooperation.

questions.prompt: How does the Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998 help a civil servant?

options.text: It lets them disclose any information to the media without sanction
It exempts them from the Official Secrets Act when they act in good faith
It protects workers who make qualifying disclosures in the proper way
It guarantees their promotion after a protected disclosure

questions.hint: Protection depends on using the proper routes.

questions.prompt: A civil servant is invited to speak at a conference about their work. What should they do?

options.text: Check with line management first so that no confidential information is disclosed
Accept without telling anyone, as it is in their own time
Decline all invitations of this kind, as speaking is never allowed
Accept but ask the organisers not to name the department

questions.hint: Public speaking about work needs prior discussion.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an authorised way for official information to reach the public?

options.text: A private briefing to a friendly journalist by a junior official
A ministerial answer to a parliamentary question
A summary posted on a personal blog under a pseudonym
A photograph of a draft paper shared in a private message group

questions.hint: Authorised routes are official and accountable.

items.title: L12: Policy clearance across departments
items.source: Cabinet Manual; Cabinet Office guidance on collective agreement and the cabinet committee system; Ministerial Code
items.body: Most significant policy affects more than one department, so it needs agreement across government before it is announced. Under the principle of collective responsibility, ministers have a duty to seek the views of colleagues whose interests are affected. The usual route for a major proposal is a Cabinet committee, which considers a paper submitted by the lead minister and the views of other departments. For smaller matters, the lead department may use a write-round, in which the minister writes to colleagues explaining the proposal and asking for agreement by a given date, copying in the relevant offices. Officials usually prepare the paper and clear it with their opposite numbers in other departments, so that disagreements are identified and resolved at official level where possible. The Treasury must agree anything that has spending implications, and law officers must be consulted on legal matters in the circumstances set out in the Ministerial Code. The Cabinet Office co-ordinates and may advise on the right route. Policy should not be announced until agreement has been reached, because announcing too early undermines collective responsibility and may commit the government to something that has not been cleared. Silence is not normally treated as agreement for substantive matters, though a write-round letter will often say that no reply by the deadline will be taken as agreement, and this is accepted only where all understand the convention. Records of the clearance should be kept in case of later dispute. Officials should also remember to consult the devolved governments where policy touches their responsibilities.

questions.prompt: A minister wants to announce a scheme that affects another department's budget, but that department has not been consulted. What should officials advise?

options.text: Announce it first and agree the budget with the other department afterwards
Announce it as a proposal, to invite the other department's views publicly
Ask the Prime Minister's office to rule, so that the department can proceed meanwhile
Seek the other department's agreement and the Treasury's before announcing it

questions.hint: Collective agreement is needed where other departments' interests are affected.

questions.prompt: What is a write-round, as used in clearing a proposal across government?

options.text: A Cabinet committee meeting at which a paper is formally discussed
A published statement of the policy shared with Parliament
A letter from a minister to colleagues seeking agreement to a proposal by a set date
A review of the department's spending prepared by the Treasury

questions.hint: It is a way of seeking clearance on smaller matters.

questions.prompt: Why do officials clear papers with counterparts in other departments before ministers see them?

options.text: To pass responsibility for the policy to those departments
To resolve disagreements at official level before ministers see the paper
To avoid the need for ministers to agree it collectively
To share the cost between departments automatically

questions.hint: Resolving issues early saves ministers' time.

questions.prompt: A proposal creates costs in future years that the department cannot cover from its budget. Whose agreement is essential before it goes ahead?

options.text: HM Treasury
The National Audit Office
The Civil Service Commission
The Cabinet Secretary

questions.hint: Treasury approval is needed for spending.

questions.prompt: Why should a policy not be announced before collective agreement is reached?

options.text: It is a criminal offence under the Official Secrets Act
It is allowed only once the Cabinet Secretary has given consent
It breaches the Civil Service Code's duty of integrity
It undermines collective responsibility and may commit the government to something not cleared

questions.hint: Premature announcements bypass the agreed process.

questions.prompt: A write-round letter said that no reply by Friday would be taken as agreement, and one department did not reply. How should this be understood?

options.text: It may be treated as agreement where that is the accepted convention, but check
It always counts as a refusal until the department replies in writing
It forces the minister to withdraw the proposal for lack of support
It lets the minister announce at once without keeping any record

questions.hint: Convention may allow silence to count, but it should be understood by all.

questions.prompt: When is a Cabinet committee the right route rather than a write-round?

options.text: For a technical correction to a form that is used by only one department
For a major or contentious proposal that ministers need to discuss
For a routine update of figures in a published table
For a matter that affects only one department and no others

questions.hint: Significant matters need collective discussion.

questions.prompt: Why keep a record of how a policy was cleared across departments?

options.text: So the paper can be published in full under the Ministerial Code
So the opposition can see which departments objected
So that any later dispute about what was agreed can be settled from the record
So the Treasury can reclaim costs from objecting departments

questions.hint: Records help resolve later disputes.

items.title: L12: Civil emergencies: the Civil Contingencies Act and the lead department
items.source: Civil Contingencies Act 2004; Cabinet Office, Emergency Preparedness guidance; Cabinet Office, Central Government's Concept of Operations
items.body: The Civil Contingencies Act 2004 sets the framework for emergency planning in the UK. It divides responders into two categories. Category 1 responders, such as the emergency services, local authorities, some NHS bodies and the Environment Agency, are at the core of the response and have duties to assess risk, plan, warn and inform the public, and cooperate. Category 2 responders, such as utility companies and transport operators, are cooperating bodies that share information. Responders in an area form a Local Resilience Forum, which plans and coordinates the local response. Most emergencies are handled locally. If an emergency is too big for local capacity, central government supports, led by a lead government department, the department whose functions are most closely related to the emergency. Examples of the principle are that a department with responsibility for health leads on a health emergency, while the Home Office leads on terrorism, though the actual assignment is set out in guidance. Where a response needs wider co-ordination, the Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms, known as COBR, brings ministers, officials and key responders together to take decisions. The Cabinet Office co-ordinates the central response and ensures the right department is leading. The Act also gives ministers power to make emergency regulations in the most serious circumstances, subject to safeguards and parliamentary approval within a short time. Officials should know their department's role, keep contact details up to date, take part in exercises and keep clear records of decisions taken in an emergency, since they may later be examined in an inquiry.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Category 1 responder under the Civil Contingencies Act 2004?

options.text: A water company
A telecommunications operator
A fire and rescue service
A rail operator

questions.hint: Emergency services and local authorities are Category 1.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a Category 2 responder?

options.text: To cooperate and share information with Category 1 responders
To lead the response to every emergency that affects their sector or customers
To approve emergency spending by Category 1 bodies
To make emergency regulations for their area

questions.hint: Utilities and transport operators cooperate and share information.

questions.prompt: What does a Local Resilience Forum do?

options.text: Sets national security policy for the government
Decides when a national state of emergency should be declared
Audits spending on emergencies by local authorities
Brings responders in an area together to plan and coordinate the local response

questions.hint: LRFs coordinate local planning.

questions.prompt: Who leads the central government response to a major emergency?

options.text: The Treasury, because it pays for the response
The lead government department whose functions best fit the emergency
The department that was first to be told of the emergency
The Prime Minister's office, which runs every response

questions.hint: The lead department principle is the usual model.

questions.prompt: In a national crisis, what is COBR and what does it do?

options.text: A forum bringing together ministers, officials and responders to take decisions in a crisis
A permanent department responsible for national security
A parliamentary committee that reviews emergencies after they end
A Treasury fund that pays out in emergencies

questions.hint: COBR is the Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms mechanism.

questions.prompt: An official makes decisions under time pressure in an emergency. Why should they keep a record?

options.text: Records are needed only so that the press office can prepare its lines
Emergency decisions are exempt from record keeping
Decisions may later be examined by an inquiry or audit
A record replaces the need to report to ministers

questions.hint: Good records support accountability afterwards.

questions.prompt: What safeguard applies to emergency regulations made under the Act?

options.text: They need no parliamentary scrutiny while the emergency lasts
They must be approved by Parliament within a short time
They apply only if the Speaker agrees
They are kept confidential until the emergency ends

questions.hint: Emergency powers are subject to safeguards.

questions.prompt: At what level are most emergencies handled in the first instance?

options.text: By the Cabinet, which takes charge at the outset
By the Prime Minister personally, from the first hour
By the devolved governments alone
Locally, by the responders in the affected area

questions.hint: Emergencies are dealt with at the lowest effective level.

items.title: L12: Complaints to the Parliamentary Ombudsman
items.source: Parliamentary Commissioner Act 1967; Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman, Principles of Good Administration; Ombudsman's Principles of Remedy
items.body: The Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman (PHSO) investigates complaints that government departments, and many public bodies, have acted unfairly or have provided poor service, resulting in injustice. The Ombudsman is independent of government, is an officer of Parliament, and reports to Parliament. A complaint about a government department is normally made through an MP, who refers it to the Ombudsman, though complaints about the NHS in England can be made directly. Before the Ombudsman will investigate, the complainant is normally expected to have used the organisation's own complaints process, so that it has a chance to put things right. The Ombudsman investigates maladministration, which includes delay, unfair procedures, failure to follow rules or give reasons, and poor communication, and looks at whether it caused injustice to the person. The Ombudsman's published Principles of Good Administration set out expectations, such as getting it right, being customer-focused, being open and accountable, acting fairly and proportionately, putting things right and seeking continuous improvement. If the Ombudsman finds fault, recommendations can include an apology, an explanation, financial redress and changes to systems. Recommendations are not legally binding, but are normally accepted, and non-compliance can be reported to Parliament. Departments are expected to cooperate, provide documents and respond promptly. Officials should treat a complaint as an opportunity to learn, put things right early where it is fair to do so, and keep good records, since the Ombudsman will examine what happened and what was recorded.

questions.prompt: A member of the public says a department delayed a decision for months without explanation. Which concept would the Ombudsman consider?

options.text: Maladministration that caused injustice
Misuse of the budget by the accounting officer
A breach of the Official Secrets Act by officials
A political failure by the minister

questions.hint: Delay and failure to explain may be maladministration.

questions.prompt: How is a complaint about a government department normally brought to the Parliamentary Ombudsman?

options.text: Directly by the member of the public, with no filter
Through an MP, who refers it
Through the department's chief executive
Through the Cabinet Office complaints team

questions.hint: Complaints about departments are referred by MPs.

questions.prompt: What is usually expected before the Ombudsman investigates a complaint?

options.text: A court has already ruled on the matter
The minister has been asked to apologise
The complainant should first have used the organisation's own complaints process
The NAO has reviewed the case

questions.hint: The organisation should have a chance to put things right.

questions.prompt: Which of these may the Ombudsman recommend after finding fault?

options.text: The dismissal of the minister and officials responsible for the decision
A fine paid by the department to the Treasury
A change in the law, ordered directly by the Ombudsman
An apology, an explanation, financial redress or changes to systems

questions.hint: Remedies aim to put things right.

questions.prompt: What is the legal status of the Ombudsman's recommendations?

options.text: They are binding orders enforced by the courts
They are advisory only, with no consequence if ignored
They take effect only when the minister approves them
They are not legally binding but are normally accepted

questions.hint: Non-compliance can be reported to Parliament.

questions.prompt: An official reviewing a complaint realises the department made an error that harmed the customer. What should they do?

options.text: Defend the department's position to avoid admitting fault
Put it right early where it is fair to do so, and record what happened
Delay replying until the Ombudsman asks for the file
Offer a payment without telling anyone senior

questions.hint: Early remedy and good records are best practice.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the Ombudsman's Principles of Good Administration?

options.text: Putting things right
Maximising department income
Minimising publicity
Following the minister's instructions in all cases

questions.hint: The principles include getting it right and putting things right.

questions.prompt: What is the Parliamentary Ombudsman's relationship with the government?

options.text: It is part of the Cabinet Office
It is part of the Treasury
It is independent of government and reports to Parliament
It is part of the Civil Service Commission

questions.hint: The Ombudsman is an independent officer of Parliament.

items.title: L12: Line management duties at EO and HEO level
items.source: Civil Service Management Code; Equality Act 2010 (reasonable adjustments); ACAS Code of Practice on disciplinary and grievance procedures; Civil Service People Plan
items.body: At EO and HEO level many officials manage people for the first time, so understanding the responsibilities is part of understanding how the Civil Service works. Departments set their own detailed policies within the framework of the Civil Service Management Code, which sets the terms on which civil servants are employed, and within employment law. A line manager is usually responsible for setting objectives, holding regular conversations, giving fair and evidence-based feedback, and making performance ratings that are moderated for consistency. New staff are normally on probation and managers must give clear feedback during it. Where performance is a concern, the usual route is to discuss it early, set out expectations and support in writing, and give a fair chance to improve before any formal process. Where conduct is a concern, the department's disciplinary policy applies, and it should follow a fair process, in line with the ACAS Code of Practice, including investigating, informing the person of the allegation, and allowing them to be accompanied at a hearing. Managers must make reasonable adjustments for disabled staff, under the Equality Act 2010, which can include changes to working patterns, equipment or duties. They also have responsibilities for attendance management, health and safety and flexible working requests, which must be considered reasonably. Grievances and dignity at work complaints should be handled promptly and fairly, and the manager should not retaliate against anyone who raises one. Confidentiality matters: personal information about staff should be shared only with those who need it. Managers should keep notes and ask HR for advice before formal steps.

questions.prompt: A member of staff with a disability asks for a change to their working pattern. What is the manager's obligation?

options.text: To consider it and, where reasonable, make the adjustment under the Equality Act
To refuse, because it would be unfair to colleagues without a disability or health condition
To ask the person to find a role that needs no changes
To agree only if a medical report confirms the request is essential

questions.hint: Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty.

questions.prompt: A new team member is struggling during probation. What should the manager do first?

options.text: Wait until the end of probation and then fail them
Move them to another team to see whether they do better
Give clear feedback, set expectations and offer support, recording it
Say nothing, so as not to discourage a new colleague

questions.hint: Early, clear feedback is fair.

questions.prompt: Which element must a fair disciplinary process include?

options.text: Deciding the outcome before the hearing, to save time
Keeping the allegation from the person until a decision has been made
Excluding the person from any appeal against the outcome
Informing the person of the allegation and allowing them to be accompanied at a hearing

questions.hint: The ACAS Code sets these basics.

questions.prompt: An employee raises a grievance about their manager and the manager is annoyed. What must the manager not do?

options.text: Cooperate with a fair investigation
Treat the employee unfavourably because they raised a complaint
Take advice from HR
Let a separate manager handle the grievance

questions.hint: Retaliation is unacceptable and may be unlawful.

questions.prompt: How should a manager treat personal information about staff, such as health details?

options.text: Share it only with those who need it for a legitimate reason
Share it with the team so that colleagues can be supportive and understanding
Keep it in an unsecured notebook for quick reference
Publish it in the team newsletter so absence is understood

questions.hint: Confidentiality applies.

questions.prompt: Which document sets the framework for civil servants' terms and conditions?

options.text: The Ministerial Code
The Civil Service Management Code
The Cabinet Manual
The Treasury Green Book

questions.hint: The Management Code sets employment terms.

questions.prompt: A manager wants to begin a formal capability process after one poor month. What is the usual guidance?

options.text: Start the formal process at once so the record is clean
Record the poor month and hold it back until appraisal
Collect views from colleagues about the person's performance
Try informal support and clear expectations first, taking HR advice before formal steps

questions.hint: Support and a chance to improve come first.

questions.prompt: A staff member asks for flexible working. How should the manager respond?

options.text: Refuse without discussion, as flexible working harms the team
Ignore it until the next appraisal
Consider the request reasonably and reply within the time the policy requires
Agree to every request without checking business needs

questions.hint: Requests must be considered reasonably.
